summary: A selection guide chart explaining how to choose the right welding process (FCAW, MIG/GMAW, Stick/SMAW, or TIG/GTAW) based on skill level, shielding gas needs, material type, thickness, typical applications, and weld cleanliness requirements.
text_content:
HOW TO CHOOSE A WELDER

IMPORTANT! IDENTIFY YOUR INPUT VOLTAGE: DO YOU HAVE 120 VOLT OR 240 VOLT?

1. WHAT IS YOUR SKILL LEVEL?
   LOW | MODERATE | HIGH (columns repeated for each process)

2. WILL YOU NEED SHIELDING GAS?
   NO-GAS REQUIRED | GAS REQUIRED (Indoor welding recommended) | NO-GAS REQUIRED | GAS REQUIRED (Indoor welding recommended)

3. WHAT TYPE OF MATERIAL WILL YOU BE WELDING?
   STEEL, STAINLESS STEEL | STEEL, STAINLESS STEEL, ALUMINUM (Spool gun required) | STEEL, STAINLESS STEEL, CASTINGS | STEEL, STAINLESS STEEL, CHROME MOLY -> DC TIG REQUIRED | ALUMINUM, MAGNESIUM ALLOYS -> AC TIG REQUIRED

4. WHAT IS YOUR MATERIAL THICKNESS?
   18 Gauge to 5/16" | 22 Gauge to 3/8" | 10 Gauge to 1/2" | 24 Gauge to 3/16"

5. TYPICAL APPLICATIONS
   FCAW: Galvanized steel, General fabrication, Pipe and tubing, Maintenance & repair
   MIG: Sheet metal, Automotive body, Tubing, Structural steel
   STICK: Pipe and tubing, Structural steel, Pressure vessels, Maintenance & repair, Thin wall pipe & tubing, Metal art
   TIG: Stainless steel exhausts, Bicycle frames

6. HOW CLEAN DO YOU NEED YOUR WELD?
   MORE SPATTER | CLEAN / MINIMAL SPATTER | MORE SPATTER | EXTREMELY CLEAN

USE THIS WELDING PROCESS:

FLUX-CORED / FCAW
- Ideal for outdoor or windy conditions
- Forgiving on rusty or dirty steels
- Good out of position welding capabilities
- High deposition rates achievable

MIG / GMAW
- Fast production (high welding speeds)
- Easiest to learn
- Clean welds with no slag
- Better control on thin materials

STICK / SMAW
- Ideal for outdoor or windy conditions
- Forgiving on rusty or dirty steels
- Deep penetration
- Good choice for thicker materials

TIG / GTAW
- Highest quality welds
- Extremely aesthetic weld appearance
- Can be used on a variety of materials
- Precise control

MIG or FLUX CORED?
   [Comparison table header: MIG | FLUX CORED]
   USES CORED WIRE: [blank] | checkmark
   USES SOLID WIRE: checkmark | [blank]
   USES SHIELDING GAS: checkmark | [blank]
   WELDS MILD STEEL/LIMITED: checkmark | checkmark (implied)
   WELDS OVER MILL SCALE AND RUST: [blank] | checkmark
   REQUIRES MINIMAL SURFACE PREP: [blank] | checkmark
   CAN BE USED OUTDOORS IN WINDY CONDITIONS: [blank] | checkmark
   DEEP WELD PENETRATION: [blank] | checkmark
   HANDLES MATERIAL GAPS WELL: [blank] | checkmark
   THIN MATERIALS LIKE SHEET METAL: checkmark | [blank]

The Duty Cycle is the number of minutes, within a 10-minute period, a welding process can produce the specified welding current without overheating.

DUTY CYCLE EXAMPLE
165A at 30% Duty Cycle
[Clock diagram showing:]
3 Minutes Welding | 7 Minutes Resting

key_facts: FCAW requires no shielding gas
MIG/GMAW requires shielding gas and indoor welding is recommended
Stick/SMAW requires no shielding gas
TIG/GTAW requires shielding gas and indoor welding is recommended
FCAW is suitable for LOW skill level
MIG/GMAW is suitable for LOW skill level
Stick/SMAW is suitable for MODERATE skill level
TIG/GTAW is suitable for HIGH skill level
FCAW welds Steel and Stainless Steel
MIG/GMAW welds Steel, Stainless Steel, and Aluminum (spool gun required for aluminum)
Stick/SMAW welds Steel, Stainless Steel, and Castings
TIG/GTAW welds Steel, Stainless Steel, Chrome Moly (DC TIG required), Aluminum, and Magnesium Alloys (AC TIG required)
FCAW material thickness range: 18 Gauge to 5/16"
MIG/GMAW material thickness range: 22 Gauge to 3/8"
Stick/SMAW material thickness range: 10 Gauge to 1/2"
TIG/GTAW material thickness range: 24 Gauge to 3/16"
FCAW produces more spatter
MIG/GMAW produces clean/minimal spatter
Stick/SMAW produces more spatter
TIG/GTAW produces extremely clean welds
Duty cycle example: 165A at 30% Duty Cycle = 3 minutes welding, 7 minutes resting in a 10-minute period
Duty cycle is defined as the number of minutes within a 10-minute period a welding process can produce specified welding current without overheating
MIG uses solid wire; Flux Cored uses cored wire
MIG uses shielding gas; Flux Cored does not
Flux Cored can be used outdoors in windy conditions; MIG cannot
Flux Cored welds over mill scale and rust; MIG does not
MIG is better for thin materials like sheet metal
Flux Cored has deep weld penetration
Flux Cored handles material gaps well
Chrome Moly requires DC TIG
Aluminum and Magnesium Alloys require AC TIG
Aluminum welding with MIG requires a spool gun
Stick/SMAW is ideal for thicker materials (up to 1/2")
FCAW typical applications include: galvanized steel, general fabrication, pipe and tubing, maintenance & repair
MIG/GMAW typical applications include: sheet metal, automotive body, tubing, structural steel
Stick/SMAW typical applications include: pipe and tubing, structural steel, pressure vessels, maintenance & repair, thin wall pipe & tubing, metal art
TIG/GTAW typical applications include: stainless steel exhausts, bicycle frames
Input voltage identification is important: 120 Volt or 240 Volt
